O R I G I N A L A R T I C L E
Yield improvement in maize for tolerance to low soil nitrogen
Sam Oyewole Ajala1
| Amudalat Bolanle Olaniyan2 | Muyideen Oluseyi Olayiwola1 |
Anthony Oluwatoyosi Job1
1International Institute of Tropical
Agriculture (IITA), Ibadan, Nigeria
2Department of Agronomy, University of
Ibadan, Ibadan, Nigeria
Correspondence
Sam Oyewole Ajala, International Institute of
Tropical Agriculture (IITA), Ibadan, Nigeria. Email: s.ajala@cgiar.org
Funding information
AfDB/SARD-SC; Africa Development Bank
Communicated by: Thomas L€ubberstedt
Abstract
Low soil nitrogen limits maize (Zea mays L.) production in the West and Central African subregion. Levels of residual genetic variability were determined in two low-N
populations using selfed progeny evaluations, and results obtained indicate large
genotypic and phenotypic variances for grain yield under both low- and high-N environments for effective selection, while heritability estimates were generally low. Ear
aspect and stay green were the most important traits contributing to grain yield for
both populations. Selection reduced days to flowering, ASI and ear aspect, but
increased plant height and yield. Yield gains of more than 25% occurred for the two
populations under both low and high N with the most significant change of 42%
occurring in one population under high N. K E Y W O R D S
low nitrogen, selection efficiency, variability
|
INTRODUCTION
Use of improved varieties and crop management, especially the use
of nitrogen fertilizers, has contributed immensely to increasing yields
of maize (Ciampitti & Vyn, 2012). Nitrogen is the most important
nutrient in maize production, and it is considered to be the second
most limiting factor for plant growth after water. Low soil fertility
and limited use of nitrogenous fertilizers contribute to the low yield
levels of maize production in the West and Central Africa (WCA;
Kamara, Menkir, Ajala, & Kureh, 2005) when compared to the global
average of approximately 5 t/ha (Badu-Apraku et al., 2013). The
estimated annual yield loss of maize due to low-N stress in the zone
varies from 10% to 50% (Wolfe, Henderson, Hsiao, & Alvio, 1988). Although increased cost and, to some extent, environmental concerns have raised concerns on the need for judicious use of N fertilizers, these pressures are exacerbated by increasing demand for
food, fuel and raw materials for a fast-growing human population
(Gaju et al., 2011), thus necessitating the development of maize varieties with tolerance to low soil nitrogen. Nitrogen-efficient maize genotypes can play a role in addressing
food security challenges in WCA by reducing the cost of soil fertility
amendments while maintaining acceptable yields and raising agricultural incomes (Wu, Chen, Cheng, Yuan, & Zhang, 2011). Significant
genetic variation exists for N-use efficiency in maize (Ajala, Kling, &
Menkir, 2012; Ajala, Kling, Menkir, & Alabi, 2010; Presterl et al.,
2003), thus making breeding for tolerance to soil N deficiency feasible and practical (Dawson, Huggins, & Jones, 2008; Lafitte &
Edmeades, 1994). Recurrent selection schemes including full-sib, half-sib and selfed
progeny have been used with success for enhancing yield and tolerance to low soil nitrogen in maize at CIMMYT (Banziger, Edmeades,
Beck, & Bellon, 2000) and at IITA (Ajala et al., 2010, 2012; Badu-
Apraku et al., 2010). Gains of 310, 380 and 370 kg/ha per cycle for
drought, low N and optimal conditions, respectively, have been
achieved (Monneveux, Zaidi, & Sanchez, 2005), with three cycles of
S1 selection for improved drought tolerance in a DTP1 maize population. Also, Ajala et al. (2012) reported yield gains of 200 kg/ha per
cycle when grown with 30 kg N/ha and over 270 kg/ha per cycle
when grown with 90 kg N/ha in three maize populations. Varieties
with tolerance to low soil nitrogen have been developed and
released (Ajala et al., 2012; Badu-Apraku, Lum, Akinwale, Franco, &
Oyekunle, 2012) for cultivation in Nigeria and by extension in the
West and Central Africa subregion because varieties released in one
country within the subregion are deemed released for use in the
whole subregion.

genetic variability is important to breeders for a priori estimation of
progress to selection (Hallauer, Carena, & Miranda, 2010) as this will
aid the choice of breeding procedure to use. This study was therefore conducted to (i) determine levels of residual genetic variability
in two released maize populations, (ii) compare predicted and
observed gains from additional cycle of selection for tolerance to
low soil nitrogen in the populations, and (iii) elucidate the relationships among traits to identify most promising ones to improve selection efficiency for the development of experimental varieties for Nstressed areas of WCA.
|
MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1
|
Test populations
Two
breeding
populations,
one
white
and
the
other
yellow,
LNTPxLNTP-W and LNTP-YC3, respectively, were formed from
germplasm from different sources. Three and two cycles of full-sib
recurrent selection for improved performance for grain yield and low
N tolerance in the two populations resulted in the formation of
LNTPxLNTP-WC3 and LNTP-YC5, respectively (Ajala et al., 2012). LNTPxLNTP-WC3 was released as SAMMAZ 30, while LNTP-YC5
was also released as SAMMAZ 31 (NACGRAB, 2014). The former
was later conveniently renamed as LNTP-WC3. 2.2
|
Experimental materials
Random plants from about 3,000 bulk kernels from each of LNTP-
WC3 and LNTP-YC5 maize populations sown during the off-season
(December 2010 to March, 2011) under irrigation at IITA, Ibadan
(7°220N, 3°580E), were self-pollinated to generate S1 families. Severe
flooding from burst irrigation pipe damaged a substantial number of
pollinated cobs from LNTP-Y C5 resulting in the selection of only
144 individuals, while 256 progeny from LNTP-WC3 with enough
kernels were selected for evaluations. 2.3
|
Field evaluations
The 144 S1s from LNTP-YC5 and six checks and 256 S1s from
LNTP-WC3 and four checks were evaluated separately at the developed low-N screening sites in Mokwa (9°18 N, 5°400E) and Zaria
(11°110N, 7°380E) in the Southern and Northern Guinea Savannah
ecologies of Nigeria, respectively, in 2011 under managed low and
high nitrogen applications. Two fields have been demarcated in each
of the two locations for the different N levels (30 and 90 kg N/ha)
as previously described (Ajala et al., 2010). Trials in each location and N levels were laid out as randomized
complete block design with two replications. For all trials, single row
plots of 3 m in length spaced at 0.75 m between rows and at
0.25 m between hills within the row were used. Hills were doubleplanted but latter thinned to one plant per hill at 3 weeks after
planting to give a density of 53,333 plants per hectare. Both P in
the form of triple superphosphate and K as muriate of potash were
applied as single doses at planting at the rate of 40 kg/ha. Soil samples were taken from the low N fields at the beginning of the season, and only the balance of N required to make up the 30 kg N/ha
was applied at planting to both low- and high-N fields at the time of
application of both P and K while the balance of 60 kg N/ha was
applied at 6 weeks after planting to the high-N field. Weeds were
controlled by a preplanting spray of Round-Up (N-phosphonomethyl
glycine) at 3 weeks before planting. A mixture of metolachlor plus
atrazine and paraquat was applied at planting at the rate of 1.6 and
1.0 kg a.i./ha for pre- and postemergence weed control, respectively,
and supplemented with hand weeding as required during the season. Rainfall amount and distribution during the season (June–October) in
2011 were generally sufficient for optimal maize growth (data not
shown). 2.4
|
Data collection
Data collected for each trial included days from sowing to 50% pollen shed (anthesis) and 50% silk extrusion (silking) and the difference
between the 2 days estimated to give the anthesis–silking interval
(ASI). Plant height was estimated at approximately 3 weeks after
silking as the distance from ground level to the flag leaf from five
random plants per plot.

2.4
|
Data collection
Data collected for each trial included days from sowing to 50% pollen shed (anthesis) and 50% silk extrusion (silking) and the difference
between the 2 days estimated to give the anthesis–silking interval
(ASI). Plant height was estimated at approximately 3 weeks after
silking as the distance from ground level to the flag leaf from five
random plants per plot. Thereafter, stay green, rated as leaf death
score, was determined for the low-N fields on a scale of 0–10 where
0 = 0% of all leaves below the ear, green and 10 = 100% of all
leaves below the ear, dead. Ears/plant was estimated as the number
of ears harvested divided by the number of plants per plot. Ear
aspect was rated on a scale of 1–9 with 1 = highly desirable ears
having clean, big and uniform ears with good grain filling to 9 = not
desirable. All ears harvested per plot were shelled to obtain grain
weight and moisture content determined using the Dickey–JohnR
moisture meter. Grain yield was then obtained as grain weight
adjusted to 15% moisture content and expressed in t/ha. 2.5
|
Statistical analysis
Data were subjected to analysis of variance (ANOVA) considering
locations (environment), replications and entries as random effects. Separate ANOVA was performed for each population in each location but later combined across locations for each N level for yield
and other traits. From the combined ANOVA, variances were partitioned into relevant sources of variation to test for differences
among genotypes and the presence of G 9 E interaction using
PROC GLM of Statistical Analysis System (SAS Version 9.3, SAS
Institute, 2011). Means were obtained on entry basis for each progeny. The expected mean squares (EMS) and mean cross product
(EMCP) from analysis of variance and covariance, respectively, from
the evaluation of each population were used to estimate components of variances and genetic correlations. Standard error (SE) for
each of the variance components and phenotypic variances were
computed as used by Ajala et al. (2010). Heritability (h2) was

estimated as a proportion of genetic variance (r2g) to phenotypic
variance (r2ph) while predicted responses or gain from selection was
calculated as detailed by Hallauer et al. (2010). Correlation coefficients were used to determine the relationship
among traits, while stepwise multiple regressions were further carried out for each population and for each N level using yield as the
dependent variable. Path coefficient analyses (Wright, 1921) were
finally used to decompose phenotypic correlations. Ten per cent selection intensity was applied to the two populations using a rank summation index (Mulumba & Mock, 1978) involving ears per plant, ASI, ear aspect and stay green under low N and
also grain yield under both low and high N to generate the selection
index. 2.6
|
Evaluation of selection cycles
The original and improved populations (C3 and C4 for LNTP-W, and
also C5 and C6 for LNTP-Y) were evaluated as part of a yield trial
that compares gains from selection in a completely randomized block
design with four replications under both N conditions (30 kg and
90 kg N/ha) in 2012 and 2013 at Mokwa and Zaria using the developed low-N screening fields and methods earlier described. Each
entry was planted to a two-row plot, but each plot was bordered by
a common earlier maturing genotype, thus allowing the harvesting of
the two test rows. Each row of the test plot was 5 m long, spaced
0.75 m between rows and 0.25 m between hills within rows. All
other standard crop management practices, such as thinning, application of fertilizers and herbicides for the low and high N trials were
followed as earlier described. Total annual rainfall (data not shown)
was above 1,000 mm in the two test years at both locations. Comparison of means of cycles of selection in each population, viz. LNTP-WC3 as compared to LNTP-WC4 and LNTP-YC5 to LNTP-
YC6, was made, and actual gains from selection were obtained.
|
RESULTS
Variance components due to environment and entry, data not
shown, were, in general, highly significant for all traits under both
low- and high-N conditions. Although the interaction between environment and entry was significant for ear aspect and grain yield
under high-N conditions, the two traits were not significant when
grown under low N. However, environment or error variance was
the largest for all traits measured when grown under low-N (Table 1)
in the two populations. Estimated components of variances when
grown under low N were in most cases, at least twice their corresponding standard error except for environment or error variance for
ASI, stay green, ear aspect but for ears per plant where the reverse
was the case in the two populations. Furthermore, genotypic and
phenotypic variances were large enough for days to flowering, plant
height and grain yield for selection to be effective in the two populations when grown under low N (Table 1). Heritability estimates for
all the traits except for ears per plant of LNTP-Y and both plant
height and grain yield of the two populations under low-N conditions were generally low.

The direct contribution of
other variable except days to flowering was low (Table 4). Indirect
effects of plant height through stay green and ear aspect were 0.18
and 0.12 for LNTP-Y and 0.23 and 0.14 for LNTP-W, respectively. The indirect effects of days to flowering via ear aspect were equally

640 kg for LNTP-W and LNTP-Y, respectively. Expected gains per
cycle for stay green, ear aspect and ear per plant of the two populations, although much lower than for the other traits, were still much
higher in magnitude for LNTP-Y than for LNTP-W with values of
27%, 11% and 22% for LNTP-Y compared to 8%, 8% and 6% for
LNTP-W. No response is expected from ASI in the two populations
under low-N conditions (Table 1). Results obtained when grown
under high N were comparable to those under low-N conditions
except that plant height will increase by 5% for LNTP-Y and 9% for
LNTP-W C3, much reduced values when compared to 16% and 13%
for the two populations, respectively, when grown under low N
(Table 1). All the parameters under both low- and high-N (Table 2) conditions were highly significantly correlated inter se. Correlation coefficients between days to anthesis and silking with ASI were the same
with values of .82** and .83** under high N for LNTP-Y and
LNTP-W, respectively (Table 2). Relatively lower values of .47**
and .73** were obtained for the two populations, respectively,
under low-N conditions (Table 2). Correlation coefficients of all
parameters except for plant height with grain yield were higher
under high- than under low-N conditions (Table 2) for the two populations. Correlation of stay green, a trait measured only when grown
under low N, with grain yield was .69** and .70** for LNTP-Y
and LNTP-W, respectively (Table 2). Stepwise multiple regression of yield on other parameters under
low-N conditions revealed that while ear aspect was the most
important trait contributing to grain yield in LNTP-Y, stay green was
the most important for LNTP-W. Ear aspect contributed an additional 8% after stay green in LNTP-W while a similar value of 9%
was contributed by plant height for LNTP-Y. While stay green contributed 3% to yield in LNTP-Y under low N, plant height also contributed 2% in LNTP-W under the same condition (Table 3). The
contribution of ears per plant to grain yield for both population was
a maximum of 1% under low-N conditions (Table 3). Under high-N
conditions, ear aspect was the most important parameters contributing to grain yield with R2 values of .64 for LNTP-Y and .53 for
LNTP-W. Days to silking contributed an additional 3% and 4% for
the two populations, respectively. The contribution of ears per plant
although significant for LNTP-W under high-N conditions was only
1% (Table 3). Although plant height had the highest direct contribution of 0.33
to grain yield of LNTP-Y under low-N conditions, its contribution to
yield in LNTP-W was only 0.14 (Table 4). However, similar direct
contribution of 0.32 and 0.34 as well as 0.24 and 0.22 in
LNTP-Y and LNTP-W for stay green and ear aspect, respectively,
was obtained under low-N conditions. The direct contribution of
other variable except days to flowering was low (Table 4). Indirect
effects of plant height through stay green and ear aspect were 0.18
and 0.12 for LNTP-Y and 0.23 and 0.14 for LNTP-W, respectively. The indirect effects of days to flowering via ear aspect were equally
larger than their corresponding direct effects.

It has been particularly effective in improving resistance to stresses such as drought
(Banziger, Edmeades, & Lafitte, 2002; Carena, Bergman, Riveland,
Eriksmoen, & Halvorson, 2009) and low N (Ajala et al., 2010). Results
obtained from this study using this method indicate the presence of
useful genetic variation that can be exploited further. Although
selection was predicted to result in an increase in days to flowering,
height and consequently grain yield, comparison of actual gains
revealed that, in general, selection tended to reduce days to flowering, ASI and ear aspect while plant height and grain yield increased. The negative correlation between days to flowering and grain yield
obtained under low N in this study is somehow inconsistent with
expectation and could be specific to the populations used or adaptation under low N because later maturing genotypes usually have
higher grain yield than earlier maturing ones. However, simultaneous
selection of many traits including ASI under low N and as used to
improve the populations implies that inferiority of one trait may
have negated the superiority of another and could be responsible for
the results obtained. Results obtained by Badu-Apraku et al. (2012)

DISCUSSION
Yield loss in maize due to suboptimal application of nitrogen fertilizers is reported to be close to 50% (Wolfe et al., 1988) resulting in
efforts to develop varieties that tolerate low soil nitrogen by CIM-
MYT and IITA. Direct selection under low N is important to improve
yield due to the exploitation of specific adaptation for such suboptimal situation. Studies comparing the best selection method to use
for low N tolerance in maize are few. Both CIMMYT and IITA have
used the full-sib family selection method (Ajala et al., 2012; Banziger,
Edmeades, & Lafitte, 1999) to improve maize populations for tolerance to low N. Modified full-sib family selection method has been
used successfully due primarily to considerations related to time,
cost and operational efficiency (Ajala et al., 2010) and due to the
ease of completing a cycle of selection in three seasons, a feat that
can be accomplished in 1 year with two normal raining seasons coupled with supplementary irrigation in a tropical bimodal rainfall pattern obtained at the breeding station in WCA. The absence of private breeding institutions in WCA necessitates
the need for public international institutions to generate broadly
adapted maize genotypes that can be used as is or improved further
to satisfy specific growing conditions. Thus, most of the varieties
released and in use in the region can be traced to international
maize research efforts of IITA and CIMMYT resulting in over half of
the impacts of maize research in the subregion attributed directly to
the efforts of IITA and CIMMYT (Alene et al., 2009). The dependence of the subregion on publicly bred varieties and the dearth of
plant breeders and other highly trained personnel informed the need
to, in addition to the released genotypes, enhance the capacity of
personnel to do the work (Badu-Apraku, Fakorede, & Ajala, 2004). Consequently, simpler approaches that can lead to rapid delivery of
usable genotypes are constantly being investigated. The S1 recurrent selection procedure exploits additive gene
action through which desirable alleles are fixed. It has been particularly effective in improving resistance to stresses such as drought
(Banziger, Edmeades, & Lafitte, 2002; Carena, Bergman, Riveland,
Eriksmoen, & Halvorson, 2009) and low N (Ajala et al., 2010). Results
obtained from this study using this method indicate the presence of
useful genetic variation that can be exploited further.

Similar high and negative direct contribution for stay green and ear aspect obtained under low N for the
two populations and for plant height in LNTP-Y implies that the
three traits are contributing to grain yield under low N. Obviously,
some of the traits normally used for selecting maize for low-N tolerance especially ears per plant and ASI did not contribute much to
grain yield under suboptimal soil nitrogen situation in the two populations. Ears per plant had earlier been reported as an important secondary trait for selecting for improved grain yield under low N and

was not picked as contributory to grain yield under low N despite
the fact that it had extensively been included in indices aimed at
improving yield for stressed environments (Ajala et al., 2012; Banziger et al., 2000; Edmeades et al., 2000) and in this study. The two
parameters can therefore be jettisoned in selecting for low-N tolerance while traits such as ear aspect, stay green, otherwise called leaf
senescence, and plant height can be used to select for better performing
progeny
before

plant
height
should only be used as a pegged entity in generating a restricted
index for selection under low N because very tall plants tend to
lodge under conditions of windy weather as prevalent in the subregion. That similar direct contributions for stay green and ear aspect
were obtained under low N for both populations, and that the highest indirect effects from days to flowering and ear aspect to grain
yield in the two populations were through stay green while indirect
effects of stay green through ear aspect were equally high implies
that stay green and ear aspect, two parameters that are easily rated
in low-N fields, can be successfully deployed for the improvement of
maize under suboptimal soil nitrogen conditions. Although the aim is to improve maize for suboptimal nutrient
condition, the same improved variety is also targeted for optimum
conditions when nitrogen fertilizer is available and used. Consequently,
comparison
of
the
previous
cycle
to
the
new
ones
formed under optimal and suboptimal conditions revealed significant
yield
increases
in
the
two
populations
despite
relatively
stable performances in the other characters except plant height. The use of S2 versions of selected S1 progeny for recombination
contributed significantly to the yield gains observed because of
changes in parental control whereby yield is theoretically expected
to double. More importantly, that yield under optimal nitrogen
application also increased considerably despite the fact that only
grain yield under high N was included in the selection index
presents an additional advantage when fertilizer is available and
used. Thus, the appropriateness of direct selection under low N to
improve yield due to the exploitation of specific adaptation for such
suboptimal situation is justified (Banziger & Lafitte, 1997; Brancourt-
Hulmel et al., 2005), but addition of grain yield under high N in the
selection index will generate the needed advantage to maximally
exploit optimal fertility environments for higher grain yield gains. The use of other parameters of the root system including vertical
root pulling strength, nitrogen uptake and utilization efficiency is
implicated as an indirect selection tool for low-N tolerance in maize
(Kamara, Kling, Ajala, & Menkir, 2002), but their usefulness will be
limited because of their association with other undesirable traits
such as increase in plant height and high ear placement and more
importantly, the level of technology and skill needed to rapidly measure and use such traits is generally limited in the subregion (Heuberger, 1998; Oikeh, Kling, Horst, Chude, & Carsky, 1999). Thus, in
addition to grain yield under low- and high-N conditions, ear aspect
and stay green characteristics under low N, two characters that can
be easily rated with limited skill, should therefore be used for the
improvement of maize populations with the selfed progeny recurrent
selection scheme.
